sources.title: Wikipedia GeoSearch, 2 km radius around Public Square, Cleveland
National Register of Historic Places listings in Cuyahoga County, Ohio

stops.name: Terminal Tower
stops.description: The 52-story tower that opened in 1930 was the tallest building outside New York for a quarter century, and its observation deck still frames the whole walk you are about to take.

stops.name: Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument
stops.description: Dedicated on July 4, 1894, this Civil War monument on the southeast quadrant of Public Square names more than 9,000 Cuyahoga County men who served the Union.

stops.name: Old Stone Church
stops.description: Built in 1855, this Presbyterian sanctuary is the oldest building standing on Public Square and has outlasted every neighbor around it.

stops.name: Hotel Cleveland
stops.description: Open since December 1918 and now folded into the Tower City complex, the hotel has put up presidents, ballplayers and conventioneers on the same corner for over a century.

stops.name: The Arcade
stops.description: Two nine-story buildings joined in 1890 by a glass-roofed hall running more than 300 feet, with four tiers of balconies you can look straight up through.

stops.name: Cleveland Trust Company Building
stops.description: George B. Post's 1907 banking rotunda, capped by a stained-glass dome, now sells groceries under the same ceiling the tellers worked beneath.

stops.name: East 4th Street
stops.description: A single block closed to cars between Euclid and Prospect, strung with lights and packed end to end with restaurants and bars.

stops.name: Playhouse Square
stops.description: Five theaters built in nineteen months in the early 1920s, saved from demolition and now the largest performing arts center in the country outside New York.

stops.name: Grays Armory
stops.description: Raised in 1894 by the Cleveland Grays, a private militia founded in 1837, this turreted Romanesque fortress is one of the oldest buildings left downtown.

stops.name: Erie Street Cemetery
stops.description: Cleveland's oldest surviving burial ground sits behind a stone wall a block from the ballpark, holding graves that predate the city's incorporation.

stops.name: Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist
stops.description: Patrick Keely designed this cathedral in 1852, and it has served as the seat of Cleveland's Catholic diocese ever since.

stops.name: Cleveland Public Library
stops.description: The 1925 Main Library anchors a system founded in 1869 and still circulating millions of items a year, with a garden courtyard between its two buildings.

stops.name: Cleveland City Hall
stops.description: J. Milton Dyer's 1916 seat of city government faces the lake from the east end of the Mall and holds a rotunda open to anyone who walks in.

stops.name: Cuyahoga County Courthouse
stops.description: Completed in 1912 by Lehman and Schmitt, this Beaux Arts courthouse closes the north end of the Mall and is one of the most complete City Beautiful ensembles in America.

stops.name: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
stops.description: I. M. Pei's glass pyramid on the Lake Erie shore honors the music a Cleveland disc jockey helped name, and the plaza outside is free to stand in.

note: Cleveland had never had a run - the rotation went Cincinnati straight to Dallas and skipped it, so it wins outright. Built from a Wikipedia GeoSearch of 199 geotagged pages within 2 km of Public Square, then each article opened individually. All 15 stops are verified standing and publicly accessible or visible from the street, and all 15 carry a street address and a looked-up ZIP. The cluster is a walkable loop: Public Square, east along Euclid to Playhouse Square, south to Grays Armory and Erie Street Cemetery, back north up E 9th and Superior to the Mall, ending at the lakefront. Public Square itself was left off deliberately - four stops already sit on it, so a player standing at any of them is already there. Dropped for a ZIP I could not settle: Key Tower / Society for Savings Building at 127 Public Square, and Huntington Bank Field at 100 Alfred Lerner Way, where the map service and the venue's own published ZIP disagree (44115 vs 44114, and 44113 vs 44114). Both are worth adding by hand if someone can confirm the postal code. Also skipped: Fountain of Eternal Life on the Mall (its only street reference is West Mall Drive, no house number), Willard Park with the Free Stamp sculpture (no article of its own beyond the park page, and no street address), Hope Memorial Bridge with the Guardians of Traffic (a bridge span, no address), West Side Market (across the river in Ohio City, outside the walkable core), and Progressive Field (address and ZIP both clean at 2401 Ontario St 44115 if you want a 16th). The NRHP Cuyahoga County listing was fetched but its rows did not parse with the usual NRHP row template, so addresses came from each stop's own article infobox instead, with ZIPs looked up per address.
